mainTopic: Consecrating a slave, מעילה with his hair, and freeing an ownerless slave
overview: The amud opens by defending רב, who holds that a slave his owner tries to make הקדש does not become holy. The גמרא says the ברייתא that makes the slave's value holy follows רבי מאיר, who holds that a person does not say words for nothing. It supports this from the end of that ברייתא, about a free man who makes himself הקדש. Next the גמרא looks at an argument between תנאים about מעילה with a slave's hair. In the end it explains that everyone treats a slave like land, and they argue only about hair that is ready to be cut. A comparison to רבי מאיר's view on grapes ready to be picked is rejected, because grapes get worse on the vine but hair keeps growing. The גמרא then turns to a slave whose owner gives up ownership: רבי יוחנן agrees with רב that he goes free but still needs a גט שחרור. רבי אבא challenges this from the slaves of a גר who died. רב נחמן explains that עולא compares those slaves to the גר's wife, and this explanation runs into a difficulty from אמימר. The amud ends with the ruling that the הלכה follows אבא שאול, and רבי זירא begins to respond on the next amud.

steps.title: The ברייתא follows רבי מאיר
steps.stepSummary: The ברייתא that seemed to argue with רב is the view of רבי מאיר, who holds that a person does not say words for nothing.
steps.simpleTranslation: Whose view is this ברייתא? It is רבי מאיר, who says: a person does not say his words for nothing.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge against רב. It says the ברייתא that treats the slave's value as holy follows only רבי מאיר.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The owner said 'my slave is הקדש', but a slave's body cannot go on the מזבח. רבי מאיר says we read his words so they mean something, so his money value becomes הקדש. רב can follow the רבנן, who disagree with רבי מאיר, so there is no problem for רב.

keyTerms.meaning: Whose view is this? A way of saying which Tanna a source follows
A person does not say his words for nothing

phrases.english: Whose view is this? It is Rabbi Meir,

phrases.aramaic: דְּאָמַר: אֵין אָדָם מוֹצִיא דְּבָרָיו לְבַטָּלָה.
phrases.english: who says: A person does not say his words for nothing.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge from the ברייתא (in the previous part of the daf) against רב.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Assigns the source to one תנא (רבי מאיר), so רב can follow the other side (the רבנן).
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The ברייתא seemed to be everyone's view, and that would go against רב.
steps.terutzMaskana: The ברייתא is רבי מאיר's view only. רב follows the רבנן.

steps.title: Support from the end of the ברייתא: a person who makes himself הקדש
steps.stepSummary: The end of the ברייתא says a person who made himself הקדש only made his value holy. This fits well with רבי מאיר.
steps.simpleTranslation: This also makes sense, because the end of the ברייתא teaches: so too, someone who made himself הקדש keeps working and eating, because he only made his value holy. If you say it is רבי מאיר, that works well.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings support that the ברייתא really is רבי מאיר. It points to its last clause. This step sets up the contrast in the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A free person who says 'I am הקדש' cannot mean his body goes to the מקדש. So the ברייתא reads his words as making his money value holy. That is exactly רבי מאיר's rule that words are not said for nothing.

keyTerms.meaning: This also makes sense. Brings support for what was just said
The last part of the source
He works and eats from his work

phrases.english: This also makes sense,
because the last part teaches:
And so too a person who made himself holy:
he works and eats,
phrases.notes: He keeps the money he earns for his own food. Only his value is owed to the הקדש.

phrases.english: because he made only his value holy.

phrases.aramaic: אִי אָמְרַתְּ בִּשְׁלָמָא רַבִּי מֵאִיר הִיא – שַׁפִּיר;
phrases.english: Granted, if you say it is Rabbi Meir, it works well;

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the answer in step 1 from the same ברייתא.
steps.raayaObject: That the ברייתא follows רבי מאיר.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The last clause of the ברייתא: a person who made himself holy made only his value holy.

steps.title: Why the רבנן could not explain the end of the ברייתא
steps.stepSummary: The רבנן might explain a slave as being about money, but a free person is not about money. So the ברייתא must be רבי מאיר.
steps.simpleTranslation: But if you say it is the רבנן: a slave, fine, he is there for his money value. But a person himself, is he there for money value?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא finishes the proof. It shows that the רבנן could not explain the last clause, so the ברייתא must be רבי מאיר.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A slave is property, so even without רבי מאיר's rule, an owner who makes him הקדש probably means his value. A free person is not property, so only רבי מאיר's rule ('words are not for nothing') can turn 'I am הקדש' into 'my value is הקדש'.

keyTerms.meaning: The Sages who disagree with רבי מאיר

steps.whatToRemember: The ברייתא that makes a slave's value holy is רבי מאיר's view. רב, who says the slave is not holy, follows the רבנן.

phrases.english: But if you say it is the Rabbis,
granted, his slave stands for money value,
but does he himself stand for money value?!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the proof begun in step 2 by showing the other side cannot work.
steps.raayaObject: That only רבי מאיר can explain the whole ברייתא.
steps.raayaSupportSource: The clause about a free person, who cannot be seen as money.

steps.title: A ברייתא where תנאים argue about a slave made הקדש
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא brings a ברייתא: the תנא קמא says there is no מעילה with a slave who was made holy, but רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says there is מעילה with his hair.
steps.simpleTranslation: Shall we say this is like an argument of תנאים? Someone who makes his slave holy: there is no מעילה with him. רבן שמעון בן גמליאל says: there is מעילה with his hair.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא opens a new question. It brings a ברייתא to suggest that the question of whether a slave becomes holy is already an argument between תנאים. This sets up the next step.
steps.deeperAnalysis: מעילה is the sin of using הקדש property for yourself. If you can do מעילה with the slave's hair, the slave must be holy. If there is no מעילה at all, maybe the slave is not holy.

keyTerms.meaning: Shall we say this is an argument of תנאים?
One does מעילה, meaning wrongly using holy property

phrases.english: Shall we say it is like an argument of the Tannaim:
One who makes his slave holy, there is no misuse with him.
Rabban Shimon ben Gamliel says:
There is misuse with his hair.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: After placing the question with רבי מאיר and the רבנן, the גמרא looks for an earlier argument of תנאים on the same point.
steps.raayaObject: That whether a slave can be made holy is an argument between תנאים.
steps.raayaSupportSource: A ברייתא about מעילה with a slave made הקדש.

steps.title: Is the argument whether the slave is holy at all?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests that רבן שמעון בן גמליאל holds the slave is holy, and the תנא קמא holds he is not.
steps.simpleTranslation: Isn't this what they argue about: one master holds the slave is holy, and the other holds he is not holy?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא suggests how to read the argument in the ברייתא. It is asking whether this is the same question as before.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If this reading is right, רב's view (the slave is not holy) matches the תנא קמא, and the other view matches רבן שמעון בן גמליאל. This is only a suggestion. The next step rejects it.

keyTerms.meaning: Is it not that...? A suggested reading

steps.confusionAlert: This is only a suggestion ('מאי לאו'). It is not yet the final answer, and the גמרא often goes on to find another way to explain the argument.

phrases.english: What, is it not about this that they argue:
that one master holds: he is holy;
phrases.notes: This is רבן שמעון בן גמליאל, since he says there is מעילה with the hair.

phrases.english: and one master holds: he is not holy?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Explains the ברייתא from step 4 as an argument about whether the slave is holy.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Whether the תנאים in the ברייתא argue about the basic question of whether a slave made הקדש becomes holy.

steps.title: The wording does not fit a dispute about holiness
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the idea from step 5. If they argued about whether the slave is holy, the ברייתא should have said 'holy' and 'not holy', not 'there is מעילה' and 'there is no מעילה'.
steps.simpleTranslation: Can you really think that? The ברייתא says 'there is מעילה with him' and 'there is no מעילה with him'! If that were the argument, it should have said 'he is holy' and 'he is not holy'!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא pushes back on its own suggestion from step 5. The words of the ברייתא do not match an argument about whether the slave is holy.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An argument about whether the slave became holy should use the words קדוש and אינו קדוש. The ברייתא instead talks about מעילה, which means misusing something that is already holy. So the argument must be about something else.

keyTerms.meaning: Can you really think that? (a strong rejection of an idea)
There is מעילה with it: using it counts as misusing holy property
Holy, belonging to the בית המקדש

phrases.english: And can you really think that?!
These words, 'there is מעילה with him' and 'there is no מעילה with him'?!
It should have said 'holy' and 'not holy'!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the suggestion made in step 5.
steps.kashyaTarget: The suggestion that the תנא קמא and רבן שמעון בן גמליאל argue about whether the slave is holy.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא's words are about מעילה, which assumes the item is already holy. An argument about holiness would have used the words קדוש and אינו קדוש.

steps.title: Everyone agrees he is holy; the question is land or movable
steps.stepSummary: New explanation: both sides agree the slave is holy. They argue whether a slave is treated like land, which has no מעילה, or like movable things, which do have מעילה.
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, everyone agrees the slave is holy. Here they argue about this: one חכם holds a slave is like land, and the other holds he is like movable things.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a new explanation of the argument. Both sides agree the slave is holy, and they disagree about which group of property a slave belongs to.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Now the word 'מעילה' fits, because the slave is holy according to everyone. The תנא קמא compares a slave to land, so there is no מעילה. רבן שמעון בן גמליאל compares him to movable things, so there is מעילה.

phrases.english: Rather, everyone agrees he is holy,
and here they argue about this:
one חכם holds: a slave is like land;
phrases.notes: This is the תנא קמא. Land has no מעילה, so if a slave is like land, there is no מעילה with him.

phrases.english: and the other חכם holds: he is like movable things.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the problem from step 6 with a new explanation of the argument.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Redefines what the argument is about
steps.terutzHavaAmina: The two תנאים argue about whether the slave is holy at all.
steps.terutzMaskana: Both agree he is holy. They argue whether a slave is like land, with no מעילה, or like movable things, with מעילה.

steps.title: Then why argue only about the hair?
steps.stepSummary: If the argument is about whether a slave is like land or movable things, they should have argued about the slave's body itself, not only his hair.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, instead of arguing about his hair, let them argue about his body!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the explanation from step 7. The ברייתא only mentions hair, which would be strange if the real question were about the whole slave.
steps.deeperAnalysis: If רבן שמעון בן גמליאל held a slave is like movable things, there would be מעילה with the whole slave, not just his hair. Since he only mentions the hair, it looks like he agrees there is no מעילה with the body. So the land-or-movable explanation does not fit.

phrases.english: If so, instead of arguing about his hair,
let them argue about his body!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the explanation given in step 7.
steps.kashyaTarget: The explanation that they argue whether a slave is like land or like movable things.
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: That question would affect the whole slave. Since the ברייתא only argues about the hair, the argument must be about something narrower.

steps.title: The argument is about hair ready to be cut
steps.stepSummary: Final explanation: everyone agrees a slave is like land. They only argue about hair that is ready to be cut. Is it treated as already cut, so it has מעילה, or not?
steps.simpleTranslation: Rather, everyone agrees a slave is like land. Here they argue about his hair that is ready to be cut: one חכם holds it is treated as already cut, and the other holds it is not treated as already cut.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives its final explanation of the argument in the ברייתא. It explains why only the hair is mentioned.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Since everyone agrees a slave is like land, there is no מעילה with his body. Hair that is ready to be cut is the only open question. רבן שמעון בן גמליאל treats it as already cut off, so it is like a movable thing and has מעילה. The תנא קמא says it is still part of the slave, so it has no מעילה.

keyTerms.meaning: Treated as if it were already cut

steps.whatToRemember: Final view: everyone holds a slave is like land, so there is no מעילה with his body. The only argument is about hair ready to be cut. רבן שמעון בן גמליאל treats it as already cut, so there is מעילה. The תנא קמא says it is still attached, so there is no מעילה.
steps.confusionAlert: In this last line the order of the two views is switched. The first מר is now רבן שמעון בן גמליאל, who says the hair counts as cut, and the second is the תנא קמא.

phrases.aramaic: אֶלָּא דְּכוּלֵּי עָלְמָא עַבְדָּא כִּמְקַרְקְעֵי דָּמֵי,
phrases.english: Rather, everyone agrees a slave is like land,
and here they argue about his hair that is ready to be cut:
one חכם holds: it is like it was already cut;
phrases.notes: This is רבן שמעון בן גמליאל. Hair that counts as cut off is a movable thing, so it has מעילה.

phrases.english: and the other חכם holds: it is not like it was already cut.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the problem from step 8 by narrowing the argument to the hair.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Narrows the argument to a specific case
steps.terutzHavaAmina: They argue whether a slave as a whole is like land or like movable things.
steps.terutzMaskana: Everyone agrees a slave is like land. They argue only whether hair ready to be cut is treated as already cut.

steps.title: Is this the same argument as the משנה about laden grapevines?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא suggests that the argument about the slave's hair matches an argument between רבי מאיר and חכמים about vines laden with grapes.
steps.simpleTranslation: Shall we say these תנאים argue just like those תנאים? We learned in a משנה: רבי מאיר says some things look like land but are not treated like land, and חכמים disagree. For example, someone says, 'I gave you ten vines full of grapes,' and the other says, 'There were only five.' רבי מאיר makes the second person swear. חכמים say anything attached to the ground counts as ground.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא wants to compare the argument about the slave's hair to a different argument in a משנה. Here it quotes that משנה to set up the comparison.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In step 9 the argument was about hair that is ready to be cut. The גמרא now brings a משנה about vines full of grapes, where רבי מאיר and חכמים also argue whether something attached to the ground counts as land. On its own, this משנה does not yet show the exact match. That comes in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: Shall we say? The גמרא is offering a suggestion it may reject.
These תנאים argue the same way as those תנאים
Land. There is no oath for a partial admission about land.

phrases.english: Shall we say these תנאים are like those תנאים?
phrases.notes: 'These' means רבן שמעון בן גמליאל and the תנא קמא who argue about the slave's hair. 'Those' are the ones in the משנה about to be quoted.

phrases.english: As we learned: רבי מאיר says:
There are things that are like land
but are not treated like land,
and חכמים do not agree with him.
How so?
Someone says, 'I handed you ten vines full of grapes,'
and the other one says, 'There were only five.'
רבי מאיר makes him swear.
And חכמים say:

phrases.aramaic: כׇּל הַמְחוּבָּר לַקַּרְקַע הֲרֵי הוּא כַּקַּרְקַע.
phrases.english: Anything attached to the ground is like the ground.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Takes the final explanation from step 9 and looks for an earlier argument that matches it.
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Is the argument about hair ready to be cut the same as רבי מאיר and חכמים's argument about laden vines?

steps.title: The vine argument is only about grapes ready to be picked
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוסי ברבי חנינא explains that רבי מאיר and חכמים argue only about grapes ready to be picked. רבי מאיר treats them as already picked, and חכמים do not.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יוסי ברבי חנינא said: the difference between them is grapes that are ready to be picked. רבי מאיר holds they count as already picked. חכמים hold they do not count as already picked.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings an explanation of the משנה that completes the comparison. Now the grape argument looks exactly like the hair argument.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Grapes ready to be picked are like hair ready to be cut. According to רבי יוסי ברבי חנינא, רבי מאיר says 'ready to be picked' counts as picked, so the grapes are movable things. That looks like the view that hair ready to be cut counts as cut and has מעילה. חכמים would match the side that says there is no מעילה.

keyTerms.meaning: This is the difference between them

phrases.english: And רבי יוסי son of רבי חנינא said:
Grapes that are ready to be picked
are the difference between them.
רבי מאיר holds they count as already picked.
And the רבנן hold they do not count as already picked.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Finishes the suggestion from step 10 by narrowing the vine argument to grapes ready to be picked.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רבי מאיר and חכמים argue only about grapes ready to be picked. רבי מאיר treats them as already picked, and חכמים treat them as still attached.

steps.title: Grapes get worse on the vine, but hair keeps growing
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא rejects the comparison. Even רבי מאיר might agree that hair ready to be cut does not count as cut, because hair keeps getting better while it stays attached.
steps.simpleTranslation: You can even say this fits רבי מאיר. רבי מאיר only said his rule about grapes, because the longer grapes stay on the vine, the worse they get. But here, the longer the hair stays, the better it gets.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא says the two arguments are not the same, so you cannot link them.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Grapes count as picked because staying on the vine no longer helps them. They only shrivel. Hair keeps growing while it is attached, so it still gains from being attached. Because of that difference, even רבי מאיר could say hair ready to be cut does not count as cut.

keyTerms.meaning: You can even say this fits [that opinion]
He only said this in that case

steps.whatToRemember: Something ready to be removed counts as already removed only when staying attached no longer helps it, like ripe grapes. Hair keeps growing, so it is different.

phrases.english: You can even say this fits רבי מאיר.

phrases.aramaic: עַד כָּאן לָא קָאָמַר רַבִּי מֵאִיר הָתָם,
phrases.english: רבי מאיר only said his rule there
about grapes,
because the longer they stay on the vine, the more they shrivel.
But here,
phrases.notes: 'Here' means the slave's hair that is ready to be cut.

phrases.english: the longer it stays, the better it gets.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the comparison built in steps 10 and 11.
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The claim that the argument over hair must match the argument over grapes.
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: The cases are different. Grapes get worse when left attached, but hair keeps growing, so even רבי מאיר could treat hair differently.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן is surprised by רב's ruling
steps.stepSummary: רבי חייא בר יוסף tells רבי יוחנן that רב ruled that giving up ownership of a slave frees him. רבי יוחנן asks in surprise, 'Did רב really say that?'
steps.simpleTranslation: When רבי חייא בר יוסף went up to ארץ ישראל, he told this teaching of רב to רבי יוחנן. רבי יוחנן said to him, 'Did רב say this?'
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא begins a new topic. It tells a story that sets up the next question.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יוחנן's surprised reaction makes it sound like he disagrees with רב, who said that one who gives up ownership of his slave frees him. This is the setup for the challenge in the next step.

keyTerms.meaning: When he went up (from בבל to ארץ ישראל)
Before him, in front of him

phrases.aramaic: כִּי סְלֵיק רַבִּי חִיָּיא בַּר יוֹסֵף,
phrases.english: When רבי חייא בר יוסף went up,
phrases.notes: He went up from בבל to ארץ ישראל.

phrases.english: he said this teaching of רב
phrases.notes: This is רב's ruling from earlier in the סוגיא: one who gives up ownership of his slave sets him free.

phrases.english: before רבי יוחנן.
He said to him: Did רב say this?

steps.triggerLanguage: כִּי סְלֵיק רַבִּי חִיָּיא בַּר יוֹסֵף
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Starts a new topic, going back to רב's ruling about a slave whose owner gives up ownership.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: רב's ruling that one who gives up ownership of his slave frees him reaches רבי יוחנן, and רבי יוחנן reacts with surprise.

steps.title: Doesn't רבי יוחנן say the same thing himself?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא challenges רבי יוחנן's surprise. Through עולא, רבי יוחנן himself is quoted as saying that one who gives up ownership of his slave frees him, though the slave needs a גט שחרור.
steps.simpleTranslation: But didn't רבי יוחנן himself say this? Didn't עולא say in the name of רבי יוחנן: one who gives up ownership of his slave sets him free, and the slave needs a document of freedom?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks why רבי יוחנן was surprised, since a teaching quoted in his own name says what רב said.
steps.deeperAnalysis: רבי יוחנן's own ruling agrees that giving up ownership frees the slave. So why would he react with surprise to רב? The גמרא will need to explain what really surprised him.

keyTerms.meaning: One who gives up ownership of his slave
A document that frees a slave

phrases.english: But didn't he himself say this?!
But עולא said in the name of רבי יוחנן:
One who gives up ownership of his slave, the slave goes free,
and he needs a document of freedom!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges רבי יוחנן's surprise in step 13.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי יוחנן's surprised question, 'Did רב say this?'
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: עולא quotes רבי יוחנן himself as ruling that giving up ownership frees the slave. So רבי יוחנן seems to agree with רב, and his surprise makes no sense.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן was surprised that רב agreed with him
steps.stepSummary: רבי יוחנן was not objecting to רב. He was surprised, in a positive way, that רב said the same thing he says.
steps.simpleTranslation: This is what he meant: Did רב really say the same as me?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge from Step 14. רבי יוחנן's question was not an objection. It was surprise that רב agreed with him.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Step 14 asked how רבי יוחנן could be surprised at a ruling he gave himself. The answer changes how we read his tone. 'Did רב say that?' means 'Did רב really say what I say?' and not 'How could רב say that?'

keyTerms.meaning: This is what he really meant to say to him
Like me; the same as my opinion

phrases.english: This is what he said to him:
Did רב say like me?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the קשיא of Step 14 by reading רבי יוחנן's question as agreement, not objection.
steps.terutzResolutionType: Reinterpreting the tone of a statement
steps.terutzHavaAmina: We thought רבי יוחנן was objecting to רב's ruling, even though it matches his own view.
steps.terutzMaskana: רבי יוחנן was happily surprised that רב agreed with him.

steps.title: Another version: רב's full statement was not quoted to רבי יוחנן
steps.stepSummary: Another version says רבי חייא בר יוסף left out the end of רב's ruling. So רבי יוחנן asked: didn't רב also say the slave needs a גט שחרור?
steps.simpleTranslation: And there are those who say: They did not finish רב's statement in front of him. So he said to him: But didn't רב say the slave needs a גט שחרור?!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא gives a second way to answer Step 14. רבי יוחנן was not doubting רב's ruling. He was filling in the part that was left out.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In this version, רבי יוחנן only heard 'the slave goes free.' His question was meant to complete the ruling: he is free, but he still needs a גט שחרור. So there is no contradiction with רבי יוחנן's own view.

keyTerms.meaning: They did not finish it (the quote)
A document that frees a slave

steps.confusionAlert: Both versions agree that רב and רבי יוחנן hold the same view. They differ only on what רבי יוחנן's surprised question meant.

phrases.english: And there are those who say:
They did not finish it before him,
phrases.notes: רבי חייא בר יוסף quoted only the first half of רב's ruling and left out the part about the גט שחרור.

phrases.english: He said to him:

phrases.aramaic: וְלָא אָמַר רַב צָרִיךְ גֵּט שִׁחְרוּר?!
phrases.english: But didn't רב say he needs a גט שחרור?!

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Offers a second answer to the קשיא of Step 14.
steps.terutzHavaAmina: רבי יוחנן was rejecting רב's ruling.
steps.terutzMaskana: רבי יוחנן was adding the missing end of רב's ruling: the slave still needs a גט שחרור.

steps.title: רבי יוחנן is consistent with his own ruling
steps.stepSummary: This fits רבי יוחנן's known view. עולא reported that רבי יוחנן said a slave whose owner gives up ownership goes free but still needs a גט שחרור.
steps.simpleTranslation: And רבי יוחנן follows his own reasoning. עולא said in the name of רבי יוחנן: One who gives up ownership of his slave, the slave goes free, but he needs a גט שחרור.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא backs up the answer by quoting רבי יוחנן's own ruling. It shows that requiring a גט שחרור is exactly his opinion.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The phrase 'לטעמיה' means a רבי is acting in line with what he says elsewhere. Quoting עולא shows why רבי יוחנן insisted on the גט שחרור. It is his own standing rule.

keyTerms.meaning: Following his own reasoning, as he says elsewhere
One who gives up ownership (makes it הפקר)

phrases.english: And רבי יוחנן follows his own reasoning –
as עולא said that רבי יוחנן said:
One who gives up ownership of his slave, he goes out to freedom,
and he needs a גט שחרור.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Supports the answer in Step 16 by showing it matches רבי יוחנן's known view.
steps.raayaObject: That רבי יוחנן requires a גט שחרור after הפקר
steps.raayaSupportSource: עולא's report of רבי יוחנן's ruling

steps.title: The ruling itself: a freed-by-abandonment slave needs a document
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא now looks at רבי יוחנן's ruling on its own: the slave goes free, but still needs a גט שחרור.
steps.simpleTranslation: Now to the ruling itself. עולא said in the name of רבי יוחנן: One who gives up ownership of his slave, the slave goes free, but he needs a גט שחרור.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא brings back the ruling quoted in passing so it can study it directly. This sets up the challenge that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Once the master gives up ownership, the slave is no longer owned. Still, he needs a גט שחרור to be treated as fully free, for example so he can marry a Jewish woman. The next step will question whether that document is really needed.

keyTerms.meaning: The matter itself; now let us study the statement on its own

phrases.english: The matter itself –
עולא said that רבי יוחנן said:
One who gives up ownership of his slave, he goes out to freedom,
and he needs a גט שחרור.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Takes the ruling quoted in Step 17 and makes it the topic of its own discussion.
steps.mimraCoreRuling: A slave whose master gives up ownership goes free but still needs a גט שחרור.

steps.title: Challenge from the slaves of a convert who died
steps.stepSummary: רבי אבא brings a ברייתא: when a גר dies with no heirs, his slaves become free on their own. Yet nobody wrote them a גט שחרור.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי אבא challenged עולא from a ברייתא. A גר died and Jews took his property, and among it were slaves. Whether adults or minors, they acquire themselves and become free. אבא שאול says: Adults become free, but minors belong to whoever grabs them. So who wrote a גט שחרור for these slaves?
steps.whatsHappening: רבי אבא challenges רבי יוחנן's ruling with a ברייתא. In that case slaves become free with no document at all.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A גר with no heirs leaves ownerless property, so his slaves become ownerless too. The ברייתא says they are simply free. Since the owner died, no one could have written them a גט שחרור. This suggests an ownerless slave does not need the document, against רבי יוחנן.

keyTerms.meaning: They plundered; they grabbed the property
They acquired themselves as free people

steps.whatToRemember: רבי יוחנן says an ownerless slave goes free but still needs a גט שחרור. The ברייתא about the גר's slaves seems to show that freedom comes without any document.

phrases.english: רבי אבא challenged עולא:
A convert who died, and Jews plundered his property,
and there were slaves among them –
whether adults or minors,
they acquired themselves as free people.
אבא שאול says:
Adults acquired themselves as free people;

phrases.aramaic: קְטַנִּים – כׇּל הַמַּחְזִיק בָּהֶן, זָכָה בָּהֶן.
phrases.english: minors: whoever takes hold of them acquires them.

phrases.aramaic: וְכִי מִי כָּתַב גֵּט שִׁחְרוּר לְאֵלּוּ?
phrases.english: But who wrote a גט שחרור for these?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Attacks the ruling stated in Step 18.
steps.kashyaTarget: רבי יוחנן's ruling (via עולא) that an ownerless slave needs a גט שחרור
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: The ברייתא calls the dead גר's ownerless slaves fully free, though no one could have written them a גט שחרור. So ownerless slaves should not need one.

steps.title: עולא brushes off רבי אבא's question
steps.stepSummary: עולא answers רבי אבא's challenge by saying the question shows a lack of learning.
steps.simpleTranslation: עולא said: This rabbi is like people who have not learned the teaching.
steps.whatsHappening: עולא does not give a real answer to רבי אבא's question about the גר's slaves. He simply waves it away as a question from someone who has not learned the subject properly.
steps.deeperAnalysis: In Step 19, רבי אבא argued that the גר's slaves go free with no גט שחרור, which seems to go against the view that a slave still needs one. עולא treats this as a weak question, so he feels no need to answer it. Step 21 asks for the reason, and Step 22 explains why the question does not work.

keyTerms.meaning: one of the rabbis (here meaning רבי אבא)

phrases.english: He said: This one of the Rabbis is like
phrases.notes: The speaker is עולא, answering רבי אבא's challenge from Step 19.

phrases.english: people who have not learned the teaching.

steps.triggerLanguage: דָּמֵי הַאי מִדְּרַבָּנַן כִּדְלָא גָּמְרִי אִינָשֵׁי שְׁמַעְתָּא
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Rejects the challenge raised by רבי אבא in Step 19
steps.dechiyaRejectionScope: The whole challenge from the ברייתא about the גר's slaves
steps.dechiyaFlawIdentified: עולא sees the question as coming from a lack of learning, and the reason is explained in the next steps.

steps.title: What is the reason?
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא asks why the slaves of a גר who died do not need a גט שחרור.
steps.simpleTranslation: And what is the reason?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא asks for the reasoning behind עולא's dismissal. This short question sets up the explanation that comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: עולא only said that רבי אבא's question was weak. Now the גמרא wants to know why the case of a גר's slaves is different from a slave whose owner simply gave him up.

phrases.english: And what is the reason?

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Asks for the reasoning behind עולא's dismissal in Step 20
steps.sheelahInformationSought: Why the slaves of a גר who dies go free without a גט שחרור

steps.title: A convert's slave is like his wife
steps.stepSummary: רב נחמן explains that, in עולא's view, a גר's slaves are like his wife. Both go free at his death without any document.
steps.simpleTranslation: רב נחמן said: עולא holds that a גר's slave is like his wife. Just as his wife goes free without a גט, so too his slaves go free without a גט.
steps.whatsHappening: רב נחמן gives the reason behind עולא's view. When a גר dies, his wife is free without a גט, and his slaves are free in the same way.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The case of a גר's death is a different kind of release from an owner who gives up his slave. Death ends the master's hold completely, just as it ends a marriage completely. So the ברייתא from Step 19 does not prove anything about a slave whose owner gave him up while still alive.

keyTerms.meaning: a release document (a divorce document for a wife, or a release document for a slave)

steps.whyThisMatters: This comparison between a slave and a wife is what the next two challenges will test.

phrases.english: Rav Naḥman said: Ulla holds:
A slave of a convert is like his wife:
just as his wife is freed without a bill of divorce,
so too his slaves are freed without a bill.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the question of Step 21
steps.teshuvahAnswerProvided: A גר's slaves are compared to his wife. Both are completely freed by his death without any document.

steps.title: Then a regular Jew's slave should also go free
steps.stepSummary: If a slave is like a wife, then a regular Jew's slave should also go free when the owner dies.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, even a regular Jew's slave should go free too!
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges רב נחמן's comparison. When any Jew dies, his wife is free, so his slaves should be free too.
steps.deeperAnalysis: The comparison in Step 22 seems to work for every owner, not only a גר. But we know a regular Jew's slaves do not go free when he dies. So why should the rule apply only to a גר?

keyTerms.meaning: a regular Jew (born Jewish, not a convert)

phrases.english: If so, even a Jew as well!
phrases.notes: He means that a regular Jew's slaves should also go free when he dies.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the comparison made in Step 22
steps.kashyaTarget: רב נחמן's comparison of a slave to a wife
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: Every owner's wife goes free at his death, so by this comparison every owner's slaves should also go free. That is not the הלכה.

steps.title: The תורה says slaves are inherited
steps.stepSummary: A פסוק teaches that slaves pass to the owner's children. So only a גר with no heirs leaves slaves who go free.
steps.simpleTranslation: The פסוק says: "And you may make them an inheritance for your children after you, to hold for a possession."
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא answers the challenge with a פסוק. The תורה says slaves are passed down to the owner's children.
steps.deeperAnalysis: A wife is not inherited, but slaves are. A regular Jew has heirs, so his slaves pass to them and stay slaves. A גר who dies with no heirs has no one to inherit his slaves, so they go free, just like his wife.

keyTerms.meaning: you shall give them as an inheritance

steps.whyThisMatters: Now the reason for freedom is the lack of heirs. The next challenge builds on exactly this point.

phrases.english: The verse states: "And you may make them an inheritance for your children
after you, to hold for a possession."

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Answers the challenge of Step 23
steps.terutzHavaAmina: Every owner's slaves should go free at his death, just like his wife.
steps.terutzMaskana: Slaves are inherited by children, so only the slaves of a גר with no heirs go free at his death.

steps.title: Then a slave whose owner gave him up and died should also go free
steps.stepSummary: By this reasoning, a slave whose owner gave up ownership and then died should be fully free. But אמימר says such a slave has no fix.
steps.simpleTranslation: If so, when someone gives up ownership of his slave and dies, the slave should also go free. Why then did אמימר say that when someone gives up ownership of his slave and dies, that slave has no fix?
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא challenges the reasoning from Step 24 using a ruling of אמימר.
steps.deeperAnalysis: An owner who gave up his slave leaves no heirs for that slave, because the slave is no longer part of his property. So, like a גר's slave, he should go free completely when the owner dies. Yet אמימר rules that this slave is stuck: no one is left who can write him a גט שחרור.

keyTerms.meaning: one who gives up ownership (makes something ownerless)
a fix, a way out of his situation

phrases.aramaic: אִי הָכִי, הַמַּפְקִיר עַבְדּוֹ וָמֵת – נָמֵי;
phrases.english: If so, one who renounces ownership of his slave and dies, also;
phrases.notes: He means that this slave should also go free with no גט, since his children don't inherit him.

phrases.english: why did Ameimar say:
one who renounces ownership of his slave and dies,
that slave has no remedy?

steps.triggerLanguage: אִי הָכִי, הַמַּפְקִיר עַבְדּוֹ וָמֵת נָמֵי
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Challenges the reasoning that came out of Step 24
steps.kashyaTarget: The reasoning that slaves go free at the owner's death when there are no heirs to inherit them
steps.kashyaAttackLogic: A slave whose owner gave him up has no heirs who inherit him, so he should go free at the owner's death. But אמימר rules he has no fix.

steps.title: אמימר's ruling remains a difficulty
steps.stepSummary: The גמרא leaves the question open. אמימר's ruling stays a difficulty.
steps.simpleTranslation: אמימר's ruling is difficult.
steps.whatsHappening: The גמרא admits it has no answer to the challenge from Step 25. It leaves אמימר's ruling marked as a difficulty.
steps.deeperAnalysis: Saying that something is קשיא means the question stands and no answer is given. The conflict between אמימר's ruling and the reasoning of רב נחמן and עולא is left unresolved.

keyTerms.meaning: it is difficult (the question is left unanswered)

steps.whatToRemember: According to עולא, a גר's slaves go free at his death with no גט, like his wife. This is because they have no heirs. That same reasoning clashes with אמימר's ruling, and the clash is left as an open difficulty.

phrases.english: Ameimar's statement is difficult.

steps.relationToPreviousStep: Closes the challenge of Step 25 without an answer
steps.maskanaFinalTakeaway: The conflict with אמימר's ruling is left unanswered.

steps.title: The הלכה follows אבא שאול
steps.stepSummary: רבי יהושע בן לוי rules that the הלכה follows אבא שאול. Then רבי זירא begins to respond.
steps.simpleTranslation: רבי יעקב בר אידי said in the name of רבי יהושע בן לוי: The הלכה follows אבא שאול. רבי זירא said to רבי יעקב בר אידי:
steps.whatsHappening: A new statement gives the practical ruling: the הלכה follows אבא שאול about a גר who died and left slaves. The last line sets up רבי זירא's response, which comes next.
steps.deeperAnalysis: This moves from the back-and-forth discussion to a practical ruling. The ruling follows אבא שאול's opinion about a גר who died and left slaves. רבי זירא is about to question or discuss this ruling, so the step ends in the middle of setting up his words.

phrases.english: Rabbi Ya'akov bar Idi said
that Rabbi Yehoshua ben Levi said:
The halakha is in accordance with Abba Shaul.
phrases.notes: This is about a convert who died and left behind slaves.

phrases.aramaic: אָמַר לֵיהּ רַבִּי זֵירָא לְרַבִּי יַעֲקֹב בַּר אִידִי:
phrases.english: Rabbi Zeira said to Rabbi Ya'akov bar Idi:

steps.triggerLanguage: אָמַר רַבִּי יַעֲקֹב בַּר אִידֵּי אָמַר רַבִּי יְהוֹשֻׁעַ בֶּן לֵוִי: הֲלָכָה כְּאַבָּא שָׁאוּל
steps.relationToPreviousStep: Moves from the open difficulty to a practical ruling, then sets up רבי זירא's response
steps.mimraCoreRuling: The הלכה follows אבא שאול regarding the slaves of a גר who died.
